paper_title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while miss the implicit user intent (e.g., "where should I click next?" while a user navigate a website), meanwhile fail to update the state simultaneously as user requests might update continuously. These limitations make them less suited to intent-aware interaction in practical. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark serving as testbed for user intent interaction, with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically tailors its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with a fleixble lifecycles via a hierarchical memory to track the latest user intent and environmental state. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over other baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intent and deciding when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation over sustained interaction, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction.

Introduction Mind is activity, range of dynamic processes of interaction between organism and world. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, John Dewey Vision-language models (Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026) are advancing from offline content understanding (Wang et al., 2025c; Zhu et al., 2025) toward continuous proactive assistance in realworld streaming scenarios (Cui et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2025; Orantqing et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025d). However, existing proactive interaction approaches are largely designed for explicit queries (e.g. Notify me when goal is scored.), and isolated, single-turn requests (Kundu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a), as illustrated in Figure 1(i). However, these paradigm is less suited to real-world open-ended settings across three challenges, where (i) implicit user intents (e.g. Help me finish this task whenever get stuck.) must be inferred from ongoing observations and interactions. Beyond identifying user intent, effective assistance requires (ii) task-relevant state tracking. As shown in Figure 1(ii), prior interactions can change the environment and task progress, making response that was appropriate earlier unnecessary or incorrect later. Although existing streaming models can retain long interaction histories (Wang et al., 2025a; Yao et al., 2026a), they still struggle to maintain an up-to-date state, resulting in repeated, outdated, or missed responses. Lastly, as shown in Figure 1(iii), (iii) user intents is evolving as the interaction unfolds (Tack et al., 2026; Tao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026d). Later feedback may introduce new goals, revise existing constraints, or shift the current focus, while existing methods often fail to update which intents remain relevant and instead continue to rely on earlier requests. These challenges make proactive interaction more than problem of real-time long-context modeling: it requires the agent to continuously infer and update user intent while tracking the evolving interaction state. This motivates three key research questions forward Intent-aware interaction: How can we construct testbed for proactive interaction with implicit user intent? How can such intent-aware interaction be internalized as native model capability? How to flexible manage context to track environmental and user intent changes? In this work, we address these three questions through benchmarking, modeling, and agentic design. Firstly, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, unified intent-aware benchmark for sustained proactive interaction with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic user intents. Building on this benchmark, we further develop StreamVibe-VL, streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents and adapts its interactions as these intents evolve. Streaming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jointly learns when and how to assist, while localized trajectory reinforcement learning (RL) focuses optimization on interaction-critical moments to improve response timing and quality. Lastly, we further develop StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent, updatable states with flexible lifecycles, while hierarchical memory retrieves relevant history to keep subsequent decisions aligned with the current interaction context and user intent. Our main contributions are as follows: To the best of our knowledge, we are the first work to study user intents in proactive streaming interaction. To this end, we construct StreamVibe-Bench, unified benchmark with 4.1K evaluation and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. We introduce StreamVibe-VL, proactive streaming video model that jointly learns when and how to assist under implicit and evolving user intents. We develop the StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains updatable intent states with flexible lifecycles and hierarchical memory for consistent behavior over sustained interaction. Early video benchmarks focus on offline understanding (Fu et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025), while online benchmarks evaluate sequential perception and response before video completion (Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b). Recent proactive benchmarks further require models to decide when to respond, often using annotated trigger points and extending to egocentric or task-guidance settings (Kundu et al., 2026; Ran et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025e). However, most focus on single intent type or environment and evaluate responses independently. StreamVibe-Bench instead unifies explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents across physical and digital tasks, with both pointwise and trajectory evaluation. Proactive Interaction Models. Online video-language models support continuous perception and low-latency responses (Cui et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2025), while real-time and task-guidance systems further learn when to speak or provide assistance during ongoing interaction (Liu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Sitong et al., 2026). However, most existing approaches center on explicitly specified requests or task objectives, with limited support for tracking interaction state and adapting to evolving user intent over time (Tack et al., 2026; Tao et al., 2026). StreamVibe-VL targets open-ended proactive interaction, where intents must be inferred from user goals, environment changes, and task progress, and updated throughout the interaction. Memory and Agent Harness. Agentic systems increasingly incorporate persistent memory (Xu et al., 2025), planning (Xiong et al., 2025), reflection (Yuan et al., 2025), and reusable skills (Zheng et al., 2025) to preserve and reuse historical context over long-horizon tasks. Recent memory systems further study how to retrieve, integrate, and abstract historical information into reusable experience for long-term interaction (Chhikara et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026). However, these methods mainly organize and access past information without explicitly tracking evolving user intents and task progress, which can cause proactive responses to drift from the current interaction state. StreamVibeHarness addresses this gap by maintaining user intents and task progress as persistent, updatable interaction states and retrieving relevant history before each decision. 3. Unlike retrospective VideoQA, relevant evidence may emerge only after an intent is expressed. Each intent 𝑖 𝑗 can correspond to one or more evidence points 𝜉 𝑗𝑘, each with valid response window [𝑠 𝑗𝑘, 𝑒 𝑗𝑘] and reference response ˆ𝑦 𝑗𝑘. An evidence point is covered if the agent responds within its window with semantically correct response to the corresponding intent. An intent remains active until all its evidence points are covered. The agent must therefore determine both when to respond and what to respond, while avoiding premature, missed, repeated, or irrelevant responses. 3.2. Hierarchical Difficulty StreamVibe-Bench characterizes proactive interaction along two dimensions: intent explicitness and intent dynamics. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on (i) Level 1: Explicit Intents, where the user specifies condition, event, or state to monitor, and the agent responds when it occurs, e.g. Let me know when the water starts boiling. We further introduce (ii) Level 2: Implicit Intents, where the user provides only high-level goal, requiring the agent to infer when and how to assist from ongoing observations and task progress, e.g. Help me keep an eye on this dish. Finally, (iii) Level 3: Dynamic Intents considers intents that evolve throughout the interaction. As the task unfolds, the user may provide multiple new inputs, requiring the agent to continually update the currently valid task state. We consider three common forms: Revision (RV), which modifies an existing intent; Composition (CP), which adds new intent or constraint while preserving existing ones; and Interruption (IT), which introduces an immediate request while the ongoing task remains active. These changes may occur repeatedly and in combination within single interaction. StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent 3.3. Benchmark Construction Task Collection. We collect task videos from both physical and digital environments to cover two complementary forms of proactive interaction. In (i) physical environments, assistance mainly relies on understanding continuous visual processes, including user activities, task progress, and emerging intents. In contrast, user intent in (ii) digital environments is often implicit in interaction trajectories such as navigation, content editing, and tool use, requiring the agent to infer user goals, constraints, and task state from the current interface and interaction history. The two settings thus capture user intent through physical behavior and digital interaction, respectively, covering proactive assistance across different interaction environments. Specifically, physical tasks mainly include egocentric daily activities and task execution, while digital tasks focus on GUI and computer-use scenarios. Annotation and Verification. For each video-request pair, we use Gemini-3.8-Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026) to clean the data and identify candidate help points with response windows, preferred times, and reference answers. For dynamic intents, we further construct timestamped multi-turn interactions in which intents may be revised, extended, or interrupted as the task unfolds. Four reviewers then independently verify the user requests and response timing, correcting or removing samples without sufficient evidence and retaining only those approved by all reviewers. The validated annotations are aligned to 1 FPS streams and converted into causal interaction sequences for training and evaluation. Details are provided in Appendix B.3. 3.4. Data Statistics Categories and Scale. Building on the three proactive interaction settings in Section 3.2, we organize StreamVibe-Bench into finer-grained task subtypes, as illustrated in Figure 2(b). The 600 Explicit Intents samples span Single Event (I), Transition (P), and Recurring Event (R). For Implicit Intents, 2,000 samples cover Guidance (G), Learning (L), Monitoring (M), and Tool (T). The remaining 1,500 Dynamic Intents samples consist of Revision (RV), Composition (CP), and Interruption (IT). Subtypes are evenly distributed within each category. In total, StreamVibe-Bench contains 4,100 evaluation samples, 20,546 help points, and 183.4 hours of video. Additional statistics and detailed explanations are provided in the Appendix B. Training Data Curations. We construct the StreamVibe-85K training set, consisting of 70K samples for supervised fine-tuning and 15K tasks for reinforcement learning. During supervised fine-tuning, we further incorporate 768K general streaming-video samples from sources including TimeChatOnline (Yao et al., 2025) and VideoChat-Flash (Li et al., 2025a) to improve general streaming-video modeling. Detailed components are provided in Appendix B.4. 3.5. Evaluation Protocol Settings. As illustrated in Figure 2(c), two complementary evaluation settings are adopted to distinguish local proactive decision-making from sustained interaction behavior. (i) Pointwise Evaluation samples positive and negative timestamps around annotated help points and independently predicts whether the model should respond. Both Gold History and Self History are considered, where the former isolates local decision ability and the latter measures the effect of model-generated history. Independent evaluation avoids error accumulation across time. (ii) Trajectory Evaluation runs the model continuously over the full video stream, with each decision conditioned on prior observations and self-generated interaction history. This setting captures error propagation, requirement tracking, and repeated or missed responses. Together, the two settings evaluate local decisions under given history and sustained interaction under self-generated history. StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent Metrics. We evaluate models along two dimensions: response timing and response quality. Timing is measured by Precision, Recall, F1, and False Positive Rate (FPR), capturing response accuracy, coverage, and false activations. Quality is evaluated using Answer Score for overall correctness and relevance, and Content F1 for key-content alignment with reference answers. 4. StreamVibe: Grounding Evidence, Tracking Intent Overview. As shown in Figure 3, the formulation in Section 3.1 highlights two key challenges in proactive interaction. (i) Evidence Grounding. The policy 𝜋 must ground each active intent 𝑖 𝑗 in emerging visual evidence 𝜉 𝑗𝑘 and determine when and how to respond. We address this with dedicated training framework that directly improves the streaming video policy. (ii) State Tracking. As intents evolve, maintaining an up-to-date active set A𝑡 and interaction history H<𝑡 becomes challenging for the policy alone. We therefore introduce the StreamVibe-Harness 𝜙, which explicitly maintains these interaction states and provides 𝜋 with continuously updated context, 𝑐𝑡 = 𝜙(𝑐𝑡, A𝑡). This separates video-grounded response decisions from persistent state tracking: the Harness tracks dynamic intents and task progress, while response decisions and generation remain with 𝜋. Details of the framework and workflow are provided in Appendix C. 4.1. StreamVibe-Harness Framework Interaction State. The Harness maintains an explicit interaction state S𝑡 = A𝑡, P𝑡, R𝑡, where A𝑡 denotes the currently active intents, P𝑡 captures task progress and environment state, and R𝑡 records previously delivered responses. As new user inputs and observations arrive, the Harness incrementally updates S𝑡1 to S𝑡 by adding, revising, or terminating intents and updating task progress. State changes are applied only when supported by sufficient interaction or perceptual evidence, avoiding premature updates from uncertain observations. Intent Lifecycle. Each intent 𝑖 𝑗 is maintained as an independent stateful instance, allowing multiple intents to remain active and evolve concurrently. The Harness tracks its current status, relevant evidence, and completion state, and updates the lifecycle as the interaction unfolds. Persistent intents may remain active across multiple events, whereas one-time intents are closed once satisfied. Importantly, the lifecycle only determines which intents remain valid; when and how to respond are still decided by the agent policy 𝜋. Hierarchical Memory. The Harness organizes past observations and interactions into hierarchical memory M<𝑡, preserving relevant history without continuously expanding the agent context. Recent information is retained in fine-grained form, while older content is progressively compressed to preserve task-relevant entities, actions, constraints, and state changes. Given the active intents A𝑡 and task state P𝑡, the Harness retrieves relevant history as 𝑚𝑡 = Retrieve(M<𝑡, A𝑡, P𝑡), prioritizing recent and task-relevant information. The retrieved memory serves as additional evidence for the current decision without directly modifying the persistent interaction state. State Integration. Before each decision, the Harness integrates the persistent interaction state and retrieved memory with the causal context to obtain 𝑐𝑡 = 𝜙(𝑐𝑡, S𝑡, 𝑚𝑡), which is then passed to the agent policy 𝜋 for response decision and generation. After response is delivered, the resulting interaction is written back to the state and memory for subsequent decisions. 4.2. Experiments In this section, we conduct extensive experiments to answer the following research questions: RQ1: How top-performing baseline behave and can StreamVibe-VL outperform them in intent-aware interaction setting? RQ2: What limitations do current proactive agents exhibit in sustained proactive interaction? RQ3: What gains does the StreamVibe-Harness provide beyond the end-to-end policy? 5.1. Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate StreamVibe across two settings: (i) Proactive Interaction on StreamVibeBench, General Timing (Yao et al., 2026b), EgoProactive (Kundu et al., 2026), and IPIBench (Li et al., 2026b); and (ii) General Video Understanding on MVBench (Li et al., 2024), Video-MME (Fu et al., 2025a), OVO-Bench (Li et al., 2025b), and OVBench (Huang et al., 2025). External suites retain their official protocols. Further details are provided in Appendix A. Baselines. We benchmark StreamVibe against representative models from the three categories used in Table 2: (i) Proprietary Models, including Gemini-3.1-Pro and Gemini-3.8-Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026), and GPT-Realtime-2.1 (OpenAI, 2026); (ii) Open-Source Offline Models, including Qwen3VL-8B (Bai et al., 2025), Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026), and JoyAI-VL-Interaction (Yao et al., 2026b); and (iii) Open-Source Streaming Models, including MMDuet2 (Wang et al., 2025d), MageVL (Yang et al., 2026d), LiveStar (Yang et al., 2025), ViSpeak (Fu et al., 2025b), and VideoLLMOnline (Chen et al., 2024). Evaluation Settings. For StreamVibe-Bench, we use the protocol and metrics defined in Section 3.5, with Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026) as shared judge and response quality scored on 04 scale. For external benchmarks, we strictly follow their official evaluation protocols and metrics. See Appendix B.5 for evaluation details. 5.2. Analysis RQ1: StreamVibe-VL achieves stronger proactive interaction while preserving general video understanding. Table 2 shows that StreamVibe-VL consistently outperforms open-source baselines on StreamVibe-Bench. Under Pointwise Evaluation, it achieves the highest Content F1 while remaining competitive with proprietary models in response quality. RL further improves over SFT, with larger gains on dynamic intents. This trend persists under Trajectory Evaluation, where RL yields higher Content F1 and response quality, indicating stronger sustained interaction when decisions depend on prior history. The gains also transfer to external benchmarks. Figure 4(a-b) shows competitive results on EgoProactive and consistent gains over other models on IPIBench. RQ2: Current proactive agents struggle to sustain reliable behavior over continuous interaction. Figure 5 and Figure 6 reveal three main findings. (i) Intent understanding remains difficult. Implicit and Dynamic Intents are markedly harder than Explicit Intents, indicating that agents struggle to determine what help is needed when intents are unstated or keep changing. (ii) Response selectivity is insufficient. Higher Recall often comes with more false triggers, suggesting that current methods cannot yet balance coverage against unnecessary responses. (iii) Sustained interaction amplifies these problems. Timing F1 declines steadily with interaction length; Revision shows sharper late-stage Recall drop, and Composition exhibits weaker content quality, indicating difficulty in continuously updating intents while maintaining multiple constraints. Correct individual judgments are thus insufficient for stable proactive behavior throughout interaction. RQ3: Policy learning improves proactive decision-making, while state tracking enhances sustained interaction stability. As shown in Figure 6(2), SFT makes the model more sensitive to potential assistance opportunities, leading to higher Recall but also more unnecessary triggers. RL further improves decision selectivity, substantially reducing FPR while also improving answer quality. Figure 6(3) further shows that, with the policy fixed, adding the Harness continues to suppress unnecessary responses and improves content quality in most settings, with the clearest gains on Dynamic Intents. These results suggest that policy learning mainly improves local proactive decisions, whereas state tracking helps preserve valid intents and task progress over long-horizon interactions, thereby reducing outdated, redundant, or state-inconsistent outputs. Qualitative Analysis. Figure 7 illustrates how StreamVibe-VL assists users in representative physical and digital interactions. Across multiple assistance points within the same task, it grounds responses in the current visual evidence and task state, providing assistance at appropriate moments. In contrast, streaming baselines often respond before sufficient evidence appears or fail to update later responses as the task evolves, yielding premature, inconsistent, or redundant assistance. These cases show StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent that our agent keeps both response timing and content consistent throughout sustained interaction. Additional qualitative examples are provided in Appendix D.2. Figure 7 Case studies of implicit proactive interaction. Across physical and digital tasks, StreamVibe-VL better aligns response timing and content with the evolving visual evidence and task state, while streaming baselines more often produce premature, missing, or inconsistent assistance. 6. Conclusion We study proactive interaction over streaming video, where user intents may be implicit, evolve over time, and must be tracked alongside changing environment. We introduce StreamVibe-Bench, unified benchmark spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents with pointwise and trajectory evaluation; StreamVibe-VL, proactive streaming policy trained with adaptive streaming SFT and localized trajectory RL; and StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents and task progress as persistent interaction states. Experiments show that our model improves response timing and quality while preserving general video understanding, while explicit state tracking further reduces outdated and redundant responses. More broadly, real-world proactive interaction may involve richer intent evolution and tighter coupling between user needs and environmental changes than captured in our current setting. New observations, task outcomes, and prior assistance may jointly reshape both user needs and the environment, leading to new goals and constraints. Future work could further study such co-evolving interactions, particularly the complex feedback between intents and environmental states over longer horizons.

A.4. Category Difficulty Across Intent Types Building on the overall experimental results above, we further analyze performance across different subtypes to obtain more fine-grained understanding of proactive interaction capabilities. Specifically, we examine (i) the relative difficulty of different subtypes for existing systems, (ii) how model performance changes across evaluation settings, and (iii) how RL shifts response behavior and performance trade-offs across subtypes. All analyses use matching tolerance of 2 s. Figures 810 report subtype-level results under the Pointwise and Trajectory evaluation settings used in Tables 3 and 7. Figure 8 summarizes the average performance of all available models across subtypes under each evaluation protocol to characterize the overall difficulty of different task types. Pointwise includes seven models, while Trajectory additionally includes five native streaming baselines. 20 StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent Figure 8 Category difficulty across StreamVibe-Bench. Each cell gives the mean score across all models available in that setting; the line spans the per-model range and the dot marks the median. Outlines identify the lowest mean within each intent type and metric. Pointwise uses gold interaction history (𝑛=7 models), whereas Trajectory uses model-generated interaction history and also includes native streaming baselines (𝑛=12 models). All results use the 2 tolerance. Trajectory evaluation reveals substantially greater difficulty under sustained interaction. As shown in Figure 8, performance drops markedly from Pointwise to Trajectory evaluation across all subtypes. Under Pointwise evaluation, Timing F1 remains relatively high at 63.575.6, indicating that models can often recognize locally appropriate response moments when evaluated at isolated timestamps. In contrast, Trajectory Timing F1 falls to 12.128.2 and Content-F1 to 2.711.1, revealing substantial gap between local perception and sustained interaction. This suggests that maintaining reliable assistance over full trajectory requires more than recognizing individual events: models must continuously update active intents, track task state, and regulate responses based on their evolving interaction history. Figure 8 further shows that subtype difficulty changes under sustained interaction. For Explicit intents, achieves the highest Pointwise Timing F1 at 75.6 but the lowest Trajectory Timing F1 at 14.5, whereas reaches 28.1. Among Implicit intents, Tool/GUI remains relatively strong, while Guidance becomes more challenging. For Dynamic intents, Revision and Composition underperform Interruption, highlighting the difficulty of continuously revising and composing active requirements. Overall, Pointwise evaluation primarily reflects local recognition and timing, whereas Trajectory evaluation exposes the additional challenges of maintaining coherent and reliable behavior throughout continuous, evolving interaction. Different subtypes exhibit distinct performance patterns. As shown in Figure 9, different subtypes exhibit clear differences in both response timing and content quality. StreamVibe-VL performs best on Tool/GUI, achieving Timing F1 of 37.9 and Content-F1 of 13.0, while Monitoring reaches only 17.2 and 4.1, respectively, suggesting that tasks with explicit operational goals are easier to handle reliably than continuous monitoring. For Explicit intents, and achieve Timing F1 scores of 26.0 and 25.1, substantially higher than at 8.9, indicating that single-event cases are more prone to missed or mistimed responses during sustained interaction. For Dynamic intents, Revision and Composition both achieve Timing F1 scores around 10, whereas Interruption reaches 19.0 and also attains higher Content-F1, suggesting that continuously revising or composing existing requirements places greater demands on maintaining the currently valid intent and task state. 21 StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent Figure 9 Absolute subtype profiles of StreamVibe-VL (SFT) and StreamVibe-VL (RL) under Trajectory evaluation. Hollow and filled endpoints show SFT and RL, respectively; the connecting segment exposes both direction and magnitude. Background bands encode the three intent types. Scores are percentage points at 2 s. Figure 10 How RL changes the operating point by subtype. Cells report StreamVibe-VL (RL) minus StreamVibe-VL (SFT) in percentage points under Trajectory evaluation. Numbers retain the metrics natural sign; color encodes benefit, so negative FPRnear change is blue. The visualization jointly exposes timing, coverage, false interventions, answer quality, and Content-F1. RL shifts the policy toward more selective intervention. As shown in Figure 10, RL consistently improves Timing F1 and Content-F1 while reducing FPRnear across all subtypes, indicating that its primary effect is to suppress unnecessary triggers and concentrate responses around more appropriate moments. The gains vary across subtypes: shows the largest Timing F1 improvement of +7.2, while Monitoring exhibits the largest FPR reduction of 15.3, suggesting that RL is particularly effective in settings prone to over-triggering. RL makes proactive behavior more selective and better aligned with appropriate intervention opportunities across subtypes. 22 StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent B. Dataset Construction and Evaluation Details This section consolidates the taxonomy, source provenance, training mixture, evaluation cohorts, and metrics summarized in the main paper. B.1. Overview of Evaluation Datasets Our evaluation covers proactive interaction and general video understanding. The former tests when to intervene and whether the response supports the ongoing task; the latter checks whether proactive policy learning preserves video perception and temporal reasoning. We describe the datasets below; protocols and metrics are detailed in Appendix B.5. StreamVibe-Bench. Our primary benchmark evaluates sustained proactive interaction under Explicit, Implicit, and Dynamic Intents. Its 4,100 evaluation samples cover ten subtypes, ranging from responding to specified events to inferring useful assistance and tracking revised or interleaved requests. Pointwise evaluation isolates response decisions at individual timestamps, while Trajectory evaluation tests continuous interaction with model-generated history. The following subsections describe its taxonomy, sources, and construction. General-Timing. We construct General-Timing as separate evaluation subset drawn from the publicly released training data of JoyAI-VL-Interaction (Yao et al., 2026b). The selected samples are held out from our training: they are used for neither supervised fine-tuning nor reinforcement learning, and are reserved exclusively for evaluation. This subset tests response timing and content quality on additional streaming-video interactions beyond StreamVibe-Bench. We apply our Pointwise and Trajectory protocols and report results in Tables 9 and 10. EgoProactive. Interaction State At time 𝑡, the interaction state is represented as S𝑡 = A𝑡, P𝑡, R𝑡, where A𝑡 stores active intents, P𝑡 records observed task progress, and R𝑡 tracks responses that have actually been delivered. State changes are represented as typed events with an identifier, timestamp, source, and payload. deterministic update function applies valid events to the corresponding state fields and ignores duplicate updates. User instructions may introduce, revise, or retire requests; visual observations may establish task-relevant events; and observed progress or explicit user confirmation may update procedural state. delivery record is created only after response has been emitted to the user. 28 StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent We enforce source-specific update constraints so that information retains its semantic role across the interaction. In particular, request specifies what should be monitored rather than what has already occurred; reference plan describes possible future steps rather than completed actions; and an assistant suggestion is not treated as evidence of user progress. Fields without sufficient support remain unresolved. Historical evidence may be exposed to the policy as context, but cannot by itself create, revise, or retire an intent. Procedural memory retains at most eight completed steps and twelve evidence intervals that serve as temporal retrieval anchors. Progress is updated only when supported by observation or explicit confirmation. For event-monitoring requests, the auxiliary model additionally extracts and normalizes evidence from causal frames within two-second window. This event parser updates evidence and event state only; it does not generate user-facing responses and therefore does not constitute second action policy. C.2. Intent Lifecycle Each active intent is assigned stable identifier and maintains an independent record of its criterion, associated event, evidence reference, and delivery status. newly registered criterion begins in an evidence-waiting state. Once sufficient evidence supports match, the criterion is linked to concrete event instance. If the policy subsequently responds, the resulting delivery record identifies both the addressed event and the associated intents. This design allows multiple intents to remain active concurrently without treating response to one intent as completion of the others. The lifecycle explicitly separates request validity from event coverage. Answering one-time question closes that pending question. By contrast, reporting an occurrence under standing request marks only that event instance as addressed while keeping the request active for future evidence. Closing an event returns the corresponding instance to an evidence-waiting state, whereas explicit user cancellation retires the request itself. These transitions update interaction bookkeeping rather than policy behavior: neither an active intent nor matched event deterministically triggers response. Skill library and selection. The Harness maintains ten fixed, read-only Skill records covering visual question answering, multiple-choice answering, event detection, explanation, hazard monitoring, milestone reporting, mistake monitoring, narration, next-step guidance, and stage summarization. Each Skill specifies request cues, evidence to inspect, response and waiting conditions, interaction cadence, and answer form. Skills are reusable behavioral specifications rather than neural models. Each active criterion maintains its own execution instance, including phase, evidence reference, event association, and delivery status. Skill selection first restricts candidates to those compatible with the current interaction type and requires non-empty observed memory, procedural context, or event context. pending question prioritizes the question-answering Skill, followed by direct matches to active criterion types. If neither applies, lexical overlap between the request and observed context is used as fallback, with at least two shared terms required. At most one Skill is selected for each context construction, and selecting no Skill is valid outcome. For example, next-step guidance is conditioned on observed task progress, whereas event detection tracks requested transition and whether the corresponding occurrence has already been reported. Importantly, selecting Skill does not imply that its response condition has been satisfied. 29 StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent C.3. Hierarchical Memory Storage and consolidation. The memory system contains three levels: recent raw visual context, timestamped mid-term summaries, and older consolidated text blocks. Under the chunked-streaming configuration, we use 𝑇𝑠 = 32 steps per chunk, consolidate every 𝑀 = 5 mid-term summaries, and retain up to 𝐿 = 8 long-term blocks. At one step per second, each chunk corresponds to 32 seconds of video. The auxiliary model processes frames from the short-term buffer in chronological order, uniformly subsampling when the 64-frame input limit is exceeded, and conditions each summary on the current request. Consolidation of older summaries is performed using text-only input. Mid-term summaries preserve task-relevant object states, quantities, on-screen text, and temporal Intervals without meaningful change are collapsed, unsupported attributes remain transitions. unknown, and the most recently observed state is retained when visually established. Each ordered transition records its temporal interval, actor, action, object, prior and resulting states, temporal relation, and confidence. The mid-term summarization prompt is capped at 220 words, while procedural fields distinguish observed current and completed steps from request-supported references to possible next steps. Every 𝑀 consecutive mid-term summaries are consolidated into one long-term block using 300-word prompt budget. Consolidation removes redundant static descriptions while preserving timestamps, distinct actions, temporal order, and supported procedural information. Each mid-term summary belongs to exactly one non-overlapping consolidation group. Once the number of long-term blocks reaches the capacity 𝐿, older blocks are evicted in first-in, first-out order. To preserve causality under asynchronous execution, summarization is submitted before the chunk boundary using only frames already observed at submission time. Frames arriving afterward remain in the next short-term buffer, preventing gaps in temporal coverage. Mid-term inputs remain available while long-term consolidation is pending. If consolidation fails or produces an empty output, their concatenation is retained instead, preserving the available evidence without assuming that generated summaries are lossless. Indexing and retrieval. Summary facts are indexed using normalized text together with stable identifiers, source intervals, and lexical terms. Repeated observations of the same fact update its observation interval rather than creating duplicate entries. Ordered transitions are indexed separately to preserve event sequence. Request descriptions and reference-plan fields are excluded from the factual index, and response records remain separate from visual evidence. At retrieval time, the Harness constructs focus string from the pending question, current request, and relevant procedural state. Candidate entries are ranked primarily by lexical overlap with this focus and secondarily by recency, with additional relevance assigned to entries overlapping taskrelevant temporal anchors. Facts and ordered transitions are selected independently, with up to three candidates from each category and at most six entries before context projection. If no candidate matches the focus, the most recent entries are retained as fallback. Selected transitions are reordered chronologically before projection. For native event-monitoring adapters, target retrieval is further restricted to at most three matching evidence lines, excluding negative or uncertain statements. No embedding model or learned retriever is used. The retrieval capacity is intentionally decoupled from the amount of evidence exposed to the policy. In the compact lifecycle projection, only the first rendered evidence line is retained and truncated to 180 characters; this line may contain joined excerpt of multiple selected facts. For pending question, the bounded fact and transition blocks may instead be exposed directly. Retrieved items are always treated as timestamped historical context, and current observations take precedence whenever 30 StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent they supersede an earlier state. The interaction policy 𝜋 remains the sole component that decides whether to remain silent or respond and, when responding, generates the user-facing text. Once non-empty response is delivered, its timestamp and intent/event associations are committed to R𝑡, while its exact text is preserved in the interaction history. Response verification, cadence gating, and post-generation rewriting are disabled.
